content: Patients with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection face several unresolved challenges, particularly regarding the most effective strategies for testing and linking children and adolescents to care. Key concerns include optimizing testing and care pathways for these younger populations and improving access to child-specific treatment formulations. To better understand the prevalence and impact of HCV, age-stratified serosurveys assessing HCV antibody prevalence and viremia should be conducted among children and adolescents, including high-risk groups such as those born to HCV-infected mothers or exposed through repeated transfusions or high-risk medical procedures, as well as the general population. Regional estimates of disease burden, morbidity, and treatment needs are essential. Furthermore, children and adolescents should be included in routine national data collection and global reporting on the viral hepatitis care cascade, encompassing diagnosis, treatment, and cure. Addressing these gaps requires collaborative efforts involving all relevant stakeholders. Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) have been shown to be both effective and safe for treating children and adolescents with chronic HCV infection, regardless of age, treatment regimen, or duration. This conclusion is supported by evidence from three randomized controlled trials, 28 non-randomized controlled trials, and 18 observational studies. The available data strongly support the treatment of chronic HCV infection in pediatric populations.
